6:36 (12" version) | label = [[Motown]] | writer = [[Lionel Richie]] | producer = [[James Anthony Carmichael]] & Commodores | prev_title = Zoom | prev_year = 1978 | next_title = Flying High | next_year = 1978 }} "'''Three Times a Lady'''" is a 1978 song by American [[Soul music|soul]] group [[Commodores]] for their album ''[[Natural High (Commodores album)|Natural High]]'', written by lead singer [[Lionel Richie]]. It was produced by [[James Anthony Carmichael]] and Commodores. It was Commodores' first number-one hit on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], topping the chart for two weeks on August 12, 1978, and also reached number one on the soul chart for two weeks.{{cite book |title= Top R&B/Hip-Hop Singles: 1942-2004|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2004 |publisher=Record Research |page=130}} It was the only [[Motown]] song to reach the top 10 on the US ''Billboard ''Hot 100 that year. The song also spent three weeks at number 1 on the [[Hot Adult Contemporary Tracks|Adult Contemporary chart]].{{cite book |title= Top Adult Contemporary: 1961-2001|last=Whitburn |first=Joel |author-link=Joel Whitburn |year=2002 |publisher=Record Research |page=62}} The song also reached number one on the Canadian ''RPM'' Singles Chart for four weeks,{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.4638a.pdf| title=RPM Top 100 Singles - August 26, 1978}} and was one of only a few Motown singles to reach the top spot on the [[UK Singles Chart]], staying there for five weeks.{{cite book | first= David | last= Roberts | year= 2006 | title= [[British Hit Singles & Albums]] | edition= 19th | publisher= Guinness World Records Limited | location= London | isbn= 1-904994-10-5 | pages= 356–7}} It was also successful in Ireland, staying at number one for three consecutive weeks. It was number one in Australia for five weeks, and reached number 2 in New Zealand.

6:36 (12" version) | label = Motown | writer = Lionel Richie | producer = James Anthony Carmichael & Commodores | prev_title = Zoom | prev_year = 1978 | next_title = Flying High | next_year = 1978 }} "Three Times a Lady" is a 1978 song by American soul group Commodores for their album Natural High, written by lead singer Lionel Richie. It was produced by James Anthony Carmichael and Commodores. It was Commodores' first number-one hit on the Billboard Hot 100, topping the chart for two weeks on August 12, 1978, and also reached number one on the soul chart for two weeks. It was the only Motown song to reach the top 10 on the US Billboard Hot 100 that year. The song also spent three weeks at number 1 on the Adult Contemporary chart. The song also reached number one on the Canadian RPM Singles Chart for four weeks, and was one of only a few Motown singles to reach the top spot on the UK Singles Chart, staying there for five weeks. It was also successful in Ireland, staying at number one for three consecutive weeks. It was number one in Australia for five weeks, and reached number 2 in New Zealand.

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
As a student at [[Tuskegee University]], Lionel Richie joined friends to form the band Commodores.  The group primarily performed [[funk]] and party songs written by band members.  Richie had grown up in a household full of varying kinds of music.<ref name=olson/>  His grandmother, Adelaide Foster, taught classical piano, and he was also inspired by the [[country music]] that was ubiquitous in Alabama.<ref name=olson>{{citation|last=Olson|first=Cathy Applefeld|title=Lionel Richie Tells the Story Behind Breakthrough Hit "Three Times a Lady" Before Songwriters Hall of Fame Ceremony|newspaper=Billboard|date=June 8, 2016}}</ref><ref name=ebony>{{citation|last=Harris|first=Ron|title=The Commodores|newspaper=Ebony|date=May 1979|pages=62–69}}</ref>

At a party to celebrate his parents' 37th wedding anniversary,<ref name=billboard100>{{citation|last=Bronson|first=Fred|title=The Billboard Book of Number One Hits|chapter=Three Times a Lady|publisher=Billboard Books|date=2003|isbn=9780823076772|page=487|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PgGqNrqfrsoC&pg=PT487}}</ref> Richie's father toasted his mother, Alberta, saying "She's a great lady, she's a great mother, and she's a great friend."<ref name=olson/>  The toast inspired Richie to write a [[waltz]], "Three Times a Lady", which he dedicated to his wife, Brenda.<ref name=olson/><ref name=ebony/> As Richie later told [[Dick Clark]], the toast caused him to realize, "I haven't taken the time to tell my wife thank you. How many guys are in the same position?"<ref name="Bronson_Page_487">{{cite book |last1=Bronson |first1=Fred |title=The Billboard Book of Number 1 Hits |date=2003 |publisher=Billboard Books |location=New York |isbn=9780823076772 |page=487 |edition=5th |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PgGqNrqfrsoC&pg=PA487 |access-date=23 December 2020}}</ref>  Richie did not believe that a waltz would fit the Commodores' musical style, so he wrote it imagining that it would be sung by [[Frank Sinatra]].<ref name=olson/>

As the band prepared to record the album ''Natural High'', group members presented various songs that they had written.  Richie played "Three Times a Lady" for producer James Carmichael, with the warning that he intended to pitch the song to Sinatra.  Carmichael insisted that the song be added to the Commodores' album.<ref name=olson/>
sections.text:
As a student at Tuskegee University, Lionel Richie joined friends to form the band Commodores.  The group primarily performed funk and party songs written by band members.  Richie had grown up in a household full of varying kinds of music.  His grandmother, Adelaide Foster, taught classical piano, and he was also inspired by the country music that was ubiquitous in Alabama.

At a party to celebrate his parents' 37th wedding anniversary, Richie's father toasted his mother, Alberta, saying "She's a great lady, she's a great mother, and she's a great friend."  The toast inspired Richie to write a waltz, "Three Times a Lady", which he dedicated to his wife, Brenda. As Richie later told Dick Clark, the toast caused him to realize, "I haven't taken the time to tell my wife thank you. How many guys are in the same position?"  Richie did not believe that a waltz would fit the Commodores' musical style, so he wrote it imagining that it would be sung by Frank Sinatra.

As the band prepared to record the album Natural High, group members presented various songs that they had written.  Richie played "Three Times a Lady" for producer James Carmichael, with the warning that he intended to pitch the song to Sinatra.  Carmichael insisted that the song be added to the Commodores' album.

sections.heading: Release
sections.wikitext:
In the United States, "Three Times a Lady" was the first of two singles off of ''Natural High''.<ref name=betts>{{citation|last=Betts|first=Graham|title=Motown Encyclopedia|publisher=AC Publishing|date=2014|isbn=9781311441546}}</ref>  It entered the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart on June 18, 1978, at number 73.  Eight weeks later, it reached number 1, where it remained for two weeks.<ref name=billboard100/> It also reached the top of the R&B, soul and country charts.<ref name=betts/><ref name=ebony/> The song was the first number 1 single for the Commodores,<ref name=billboard100/> and the first of their songs to be a top 10 hit in the United Kingdom.<ref name=betts/>   The song eventually reached the top of charts in the United Kingdom, South Africa, and Canada, and was in the top 5 on charts in 25 other countries.<ref name=ebony/>

''[[Record World]]'' called it a "[[sentimental ballad]]" that should make the pop adult charts as well as the R&B charts.<ref name=rw>{{cite magazine|magazine=Record World|date=June 17, 1978|accessdate=2023-02-13|title=Hits of the Week|page=1|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/78/RW-1978-06-17.pdf}}</ref>

The original Commodores' version of the song was included as the final track on Lionel Richie's greatest hits [[compilation album]] ''[[Back to Front (Lionel Richie album)|Back to Front]]'', released in 1992.
sections.text:
In the United States, "Three Times a Lady" was the first of two singles off of Natural High.  It entered the Billboard Hot 100 chart on June 18, 1978, at number 73.  Eight weeks later, it reached number 1, where it remained for two weeks. It also reached the top of the R&B, soul and country charts. The song was the first number 1 single for the Commodores, and the first of their songs to be a top 10 hit in the United Kingdom.   The song eventually reached the top of charts in the United Kingdom, South Africa, and Canada, and was in the top 5 on charts in 25 other countries.

Record World called it a "sentimental ballad" that should make the pop adult charts as well as the R&B charts.

The original Commodores' version of the song was included as the final track on Lionel Richie's greatest hits compilation album Back to Front, released in 1992.

sections.heading: Impact
sections.wikitext:
The song was a "smash hit"<ref name=olson/> which launched the Commodores into a higher level of fame and notice.  In large part due to the popularity of this song, the band was named the top R&B group of the year by ''[[Rolling Stone]]'', ''Billboard'', and ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]''.  ''Billboard'' also named them the number 3 pop group of 1978, making them one of the historically few non-white performers listed.<ref name=ebony/> "Three Times a Lady" was nominated for two [[Grammy]] awards, for Song of the Year and for Best Pop Vocal Performance by a Duo, Group, or Chorus.<ref name=grammy>{{citation|title=Artist: Commodores|publisher=Grammy Awards|url=https://www.grammy.com/artists/commodores/15797|access-date=3 April 2019}}</ref>  The song won a 1979 [[American Music Award]] and a [[People's Choice Award]].<ref>{{citation|title=From Commodores lead to global solo sensation, a spectacular 50-year career|publisher=Songwriters Hall of Fame|url=https://www.songhall.org/profile/Lionel_Richie|access-date=3 April 2019}}</ref>

Many other artists reached out to Richie, asking him to write songs with them.  Richie at first turned them all down, but eventually agreed to work with country singer [[Kenny Rogers]].  The collaboration resulted in Rogers' hit song "[[Lady (Kenny Rogers song)|Lady]]".<ref name=betts/>
sections.text:
The song was a "smash hit" which launched the Commodores into a higher level of fame and notice.  In large part due to the popularity of this song, the band was named the top R&B group of the year by Rolling Stone, Billboard, and Cashbox.  Billboard also named them the number 3 pop group of 1978, making them one of the historically few non-white performers listed. "Three Times a Lady" was nominated for two Grammy awards, for Song of the Year and for Best Pop Vocal Performance by a Duo, Group, or Chorus.  The song won a 1979 American Music Award and a People's Choice Award.

Many other artists reached out to Richie, asking him to write songs with them.  Richie at first turned them all down, but eventually agreed to work with country singer Kenny Rogers.  The collaboration resulted in Rogers' hit song "Lady".

Twitty's version reached number 7 on the ''Billboard'' [[Hot Country Songs|Hot Country Singles]] chart in the late winter of 1984 and number 4 in the Canadian charts.{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.6307.pdf| title=RPM Country 50 Singles - March 31, 1984}} (#81 Year End{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/obj/028020/f2/nlc008388.9648.pdf| title=RPM Top 100 Country of 1984 - January 5, 1985}}) [[AllMusic]] reviewer Tom Jurek wrote that "Three Times a Lady" and the previous single, "[[Heartache Tonight]]" "offer(ed) a solid view of Twitty's amazing crossover potential, and his ability to take well-known pop tracks and turn them into solid country smashes long after the countrypolitan days of [[Chet Atkins]] and RCA."{{cite web|first=Thom |last=Jurek |url=http://allmusic.com/album/lost-in-the-feeling-r567287/review |title=Lost in the Feeling - Conway Twitty | Songs, Reviews, Credits, Awards |publisher=AllMusic |access-date=2014-03-28}}
